management_paragraphs: For 2026, the adopted ABC and OFL are 2,036,000 and 2,496,000 t. The Bering Sea subarea TAC increased from 1,375,000 to 1,389,500 t after inseason reallocations. The August allocations included 139,400 t for Community Development Quota (CDQ) directed fishing and 46,000 t for incidental catch. Bering Sea catch totals include CDQ directed catch and incidental catch, including incidental CDQ catch. Bogoslof and Aleutian Islands catches are reported separately (National Marine Fisheries Service 2026a, 2026c).

The directed pollock allowance is allocated 45% to the A season (January 20–June 10) and 55% to the B season (June 10–November 1). The non-CDQ allowance is divided among the inshore (50%), catcher/processor (40%) and mothership (10%) sectors. In the Steller sea lion conservation area, each sector may catch up to 28% of its annual directed allowance before noon April 1 (National Marine Fisheries Service 2026a). The Winter Herring Savings Area (58–60° N, 172–175° W) is closed to directed pollock trawling, including CDQ fishing, from September 30, 2026, to March 1, 2027 (National Marine Fisheries Service 2026b).

Area restrictions, allocations, monitoring, and incentives are used to reduce prohibited species catch in the EBS pollock fishery. Table 2 summarizes major management changes. Industry cooperatives use rolling-hotspot closures to move fishing away from areas of high salmon bycatch. These voluntary programs began for chum salmon in 2001 and Chinook salmon in 2002. Amendment 84, implemented in 2007, allowed participating vessels to use approved intercooperative bycatch-reduction agreements in place of specified fixed salmon-area closures (National Marine Fisheries Service 2007, 2023).

Amendment 91 established Chinook salmon bycatch limits and incentives to reduce bycatch while allowing the pollock TAC to be harvested. Implemented in the 2011 fishery, it combined a 60,000-fish annual prohibited species catch (PSC) limit with incentive plan agreements and a 47,591-fish performance standard. A sector that exceeds its share of the standard in three of seven consecutive years receives a lower allocation in all subsequent years. Amendment 110, implemented in 2016, strengthened Chinook and chum avoidance and tied Chinook limits to salmon returns in western Alaska. When the State of Alaska’s index for the Kuskokwim, Unalakleet and Upper Yukon systems is 250,000 fish or less, the following year’s PSC limit and performance standard fall to 45,000 and 33,318 fish, respectively. The index first applied to the 2017 fishery (National Marine Fisheries Service 2010, 2016).

NOAA Fisheries’ North Pacific Groundfish and Halibut Observer Program provides the salmon counts used to monitor PSC limits in the Bering Sea pollock fishery. Regulations require vessels to retain salmon until observers can count them at at-sea processors or during offloading. Catcher vessels carry an observer or an electronic monitoring (EM) system, and shoreside observers count salmon in deliveries (National Marine Fisheries Service Alaska Regional Office 2025). The Alaska Fisheries Science Center’s Genetics Program analyzes tissue samples collected by observers to identify the salmon stocks caught as bycatch. These stock-composition estimates help assess impacts on salmon populations and guide avoidance measures (NOAA Fisheries salmon bycatch monitoring). Genetic sampling of the 2015 Chinook bycatch is described by (Guthrie et al. 2017).

paragraphs.Catch by area and season is summarized: Catch by area and season is summarized in Table 3. The catch as of October 17, 2026, was 1,267,543 t: 604,041 t in the A season and 663,501 t in the B season.
paragraphs.The annual catch-accounting extract summ: Table 4 summarizes annual retained and discarded catch. The 2026 total is 1,312,505 t, including 8,997 t discarded (0.7%).
